text: We've covered constraints that guarantee identity and uniqueness. Now the two simplest, and in some ways most important: NOT NULL and CHECK.
NOT NULL requires a value — full stop. Every column is nullable by default in T-SQL unless you explicitly say otherwise. It's the simplest constraint in the whole language: no value, no row.

A CHECK constraint goes further. It doesn't just ask is there a value — it validates that the value satisfies any boolean expression you write. Here's a real one from AdventureWorks's Production dot Product table: list price can never be negative.

CHECK constraints can enforce a list of valid values too — also real, from that same table: a product's class code has to be L, M, or H, or unknown. Ranges, lists, pattern matching — any logic on that row, checked automatically on every insert and update.

Here's why this matters more than it might seem. Any application form could validate that a price isn't negative — but if even one code path forgets, bad data gets in, silently, forever. A CHECK constraint makes that physically impossible to bypass, no matter what wrote the insert.
Require a value, then validate it — two of your simplest, sturdiest tools. Next lesson: the first of three relationship shapes between tables, starting with one-to-one. See you there.
